About.title: What are Runes?
About.subtitle: A protocol for creating and moving fungible tokens directly on Bitcoin — lightweight, with no smart contracts and no junk UTXOs.
About.fact_launch: Launched at the April 20, 2024 halving · block 840,000
About.basics_lead: Created by Casey Rodarmor, the author of Ordinals, Runes use nothing but what Bitcoin already offers.
About.basics_utxo_text: Rune balances are attached to Bitcoin transaction outputs (UTXOs), like labels on coins. When the coin is spent, the runes move wherever the transaction sends them. No contract keeps the balances.
About.basics_runestone_text: Each operation is written in a “runestone”: an OP_RETURN output tagged with OP_13 and a few bytes of data. OP_RETURN outputs can’t be spent, so they never enter the UTXO set that nodes have to keep.
About.basics_indexer_text: Bitcoin nodes don’t interpret runes. Indexers such as ord or UniSat’s read every runestone since block 840,000 and work out who owns what. The balances you see here come from one of them.
About.lifecycle_lead: Everything happens in ordinary Bitcoin transactions, with a runestone saying what to do.
About.lifecycle_etch_text: The creator sets the name, symbol, decimals, how much they keep (premine) and the mint rules. So nobody can grab the name first, it must be committed in an earlier transaction with at least 6 confirmations.
About.lifecycle_mint_text: If the rune has an open mint, anyone can mint a fixed amount per transaction until the mint cap or the deadline set at etching is reached.
About.lifecycle_transfer_text: Instructions called edicts say how much of each rune goes to each output. Anything left unassigned goes to the first non-OP_RETURN output, usually the change.
About.lifecycle_burn_text: Runes sent to an OP_RETURN output are burned on purpose. A malformed runestone becomes a “cenotaph”, and the runes in the transaction’s inputs are burned by accident.
About.anatomy_lead: Live data from {name}, one of the first runes, etched in the launch block.
About.anatomy_name_hint: Letters A to Z only. The dots (•) are spacers that make it readable; the unique name is {rune}.
About.anatomy_symbol_hint: A single character used as the rune’s currency sign. Without one, ¤ is used.
About.anatomy_id_hint: Block {block, number} and position {tx} of the etching transaction within it. Look-alike names can fool you; the ID is unique.
About.anatomy_divisibility_hint: 1 unit splits into {units, number} parts, like 1 BTC into 100,000,000 sats.
About.anatomy_supply_hint: Total amount in existence: premine plus mints.
About.anatomy_premine_hint_all: The whole supply went to the creator at etching; there was no public mint.
About.anatomy_premine_hint_mint: The rest was distributed through a public mint.
About.compare_lead: Three ways to make tokens, side by side.
About.compare_balances_brc20: Only in the indexer, derived from inscriptions
About.compare_data_brc20: JSON text inscribed in the transaction (Ordinals)
About.compare_transfer_brc20: 2 transactions: inscribe the transfer, then send it
About.compare_utxos_runes: No: it uses the transaction’s normal outputs
About.compare_utxos_brc20: Yes, each inscription takes a UTXO
About.compare_note: BRC-20 pioneered Bitcoin tokens in 2023 and is still active. Runes came along to do the same more lightly, using Bitcoin’s own UTXO model.
About.app_text: It’s a dashboard for following Runes: enter a Bitcoin address to see its balances, history and dollar value, and explore the market with prices, charts and sales for each rune.
About.app_read_only: Read-only: we never ask for private keys, seed phrases or signatures.
About.source_unisat_use: Rune indexer (balances, holders, supply) and market (prices and sales)
About.source_coingecko_use: Portfolio prices and price change for the runes it tracks
About.source_binance_use: BTC price history, for the chart and to convert sales into dollars
About.source_mempool_use: Transactions and confirmations for your address
